summary: Crescent City sits closer to the Oregon border than to any California city most people could name on a map — the drive south to San Francisco covers roughly 350 miles of winding coastal highway, making this one of the most geographically isolated towns in the state. That remoteness is inseparable from what defines daily life here: the rugged Pacific coastline, the immediate proximity to Redwoods National and State Parks, and a year-round climate so temperate it barely fluctuates, with average highs around 60°F and lows near 50°F across seasons — no scorching summers, no freezing winters, just persistent cool marine air and fog. The local economy leans heavily on public-sector and healthcare roles tied to the county seat and Sutter Coast Hospital, plus fishing and timber — there is no large private-sector employer base to hop between. A median household income of roughly $41,000 against a median home price near $290,500 yields a price-to-income ratio above 7:1, which is steep but still dramatically cheaper than coastal California norms; rents averaging $1,127 consume a significant share of that income. The town spans just 2.4 square miles, compact enough that most errands happen within a short drive or bike ride, and Battery Point Lighthouse and the harbor give evening walks genuine coastal drama. Property crime rates run high — larceny alone tops 5,400 per 100,000 — a pattern common in small tourist-adjacent towns with seasonal economic swings. Crescent City is essentially a small, cool, fog-wrapped outpost where affordable Pacific-coast living and world-class redwood access come packaged with real economic constraints and deep geographic isolation.
